prompt: Sam Lewis's 'top six' things employees value include all EXCEPT:
explanation: The six: Challenge · Location · Advancement · Money · People · Security.
source: MC Bank #94 · Question Bank PDF p. 12; key p. 19

prompt: Lewis hired a woman for LESS money because she hated her boss. Which value outweighed money?
explanation: People = who you work with and for.
source: MC Bank #95 · Question Bank PDF p. 12; key p. 19

prompt: Lewis called which value the 'sneaky' one that's at the top of many lists without people realizing it?
explanation: Some people won't move for any amount of money.
source: MC Bank #96 · Question Bank PDF p. 12; key p. 19

prompt: Which value matters most EARLY in a career, when a flat org chart means 'I'm not going anywhere'?
explanation: Priorities shift over a career.
source: MC Bank #97 · Question Bank PDF p. 12; key p. 19

prompt: Raises given for each additional year on the job fit which of Lewis's three compensation models?
explanation: His 3 models: time & tenure · performance · competency. Most good systems combine all three.
source: MC Bank #98 · Question Bank PDF p. 12; key p. 19

prompt: Lewis's 'manager's test' for seniority pay asks:
options: What does an additional year of experience change in this role?
explanation: If an extra year changes nothing, pay stays put. The job is the limiter, not the person.
source: MC Bank #99 · Question Bank PDF p. 12; key p. 19

prompt: Output jumped after new equipment was installed, and workers want the productivity bonus. Which performance-pay test does this fail?
explanation: The 4 tests: Influence · Clarity · Balance · Baseline. The workers didn't cause the gain. (New equipment also shifts the baseline.)
source: MC Bank #100 · Question Bank PDF p. 12; key p. 19

prompt: A line runs at 110% of rate but produces 80% scrap because the bonus only rewards speed. Which test does it fail?
explanation: Balance: the measure can't reward one result (speed) at the expense of another (quality).
source: MC Bank #101 · Question Bank PDF p. 12; key p. 19

prompt: A bonus target is set using the 2008 housing crash as the starting year. Which test does it fail?
explanation: A bad starting year makes the targets far too easy.
source: MC Bank #102 · Question Bank PDF p. 13; key p. 19

prompt: Lewis held 8 meetings a month, including one at 11 p.m., to explain how the bonus was calculated. Which test was he addressing?
explanation: People must understand how the payout is calculated.
source: MC Bank #103 · Question Bank PDF p. 13; key p. 19

prompt: Lewis's plant-wide STAR bonus (productivity + quality + expenses, with everyone in the pool) was modeled on the:
explanation: Gainsharing. He also cited Herzberg and open-book management, and he prefers bonuses for smaller groups.
source: MC Bank #104 · Question Bank PDF p. 13; key p. 19

prompt: Extruder operators got a raise for certifying on the calender line, but nobody was ever moved there. Which competency test does this fail?
explanation: The 3 competency tests: Relevant · Applied · Used. The company never used the skill, so he eliminated the pay.
source: MC Bank #105 · Question Bank PDF p. 13; key p. 19

prompt: All maintenance workers were paid for hydraulics training, but a later evaluation showed almost nobody could actually do it. Which test does this fail?
explanation: Lesson: evaluate first, then pay.
source: MC Bank #106 · Question Bank PDF p. 13; key p. 19

prompt: According to Lewis, pay rises as a job shifts from managing:
explanation: Entry level = things, managers = people, CEO = mostly ideas. This ties to point systems like Hay.
source: MC Bank #107 · Question Bank PDF p. 13; key p. 19

prompt: A company offers an individual bonus per completed work order. The most likely unintended consequence is:
options: Cherry-picking easy orders and rushed repairs
explanation: You also get no teamwork and no teaching. Lewis's fix was a 4-tier maintenance pay system that rewarded seniors for bringing up the next tier.
source: MC Bank #108 · Question Bank PDF p. 13; key p. 19

prompt: Senior 'wizard' technicians won't share their 'little black book' of knowledge because it protects their:
explanation: Knowledge = power = job security. The answer is to reward mentoring through tiered, skill-based pay.
source: MC Bank #109 · Question Bank PDF p. 13; key p. 19

prompt: Rivian entered Normal at $17/hr, quickly went to $22, and forced local plants to raise pay. This shows:
options: A labor-market shock driving external competitiveness
explanation: Lewis told clients: 'Your pay has to go up.'
source: MC Bank #110 · Question Bank PDF p. 14; key p. 19

prompt: Per Lewis, a salary survey does NOT tell you:
options: Whether you're in the right range
Whether your rewards support the right behavior
explanation: Surveys only answer the competitiveness question. They also don't tell you what different employees value.
source: MC Bank #111 · Question Bank PDF p. 14; key p. 20

prompt: Cracker Barrel's star pins for servers are an example of which total-rewards element?
explanation: The total rewards portfolio: cash · benefits · flexibility · growth opportunities · recognition. The goal is to send employees a coherent signal.
source: MC Bank #112 · Question Bank PDF p. 14; key p. 20

prompt: Lewis used the DISC analogy to make which point about comp design?
options: Design comp for the whole team, not one type of person
Use personality tests to set pay
explanation: A room full of one type doesn't work (the Jordan vs. Riley example).
source: MC Bank #113 · Question Bank PDF p. 14; key p. 20

prompt: Performance pay fails when employees can't influence the result. Competency pay fails when:
explanation: This is the 'common trap' line from the Lewis notes. Also: don't pay a PhD rocket scientist to assemble widgets.
source: MC Bank #114 · Question Bank PDF p. 14; key p. 20
